verses.text: Yahweh spoke to Moses and to Aaron, saying,

“When a man shall have a rising in his body’s skin, or a scab, or a bright spot, and it becomes in the skin of his body the plague of leprosy, then he shall be brought to Aaron the priest, or to one of his sons, the priests:

and the priest shall examine the plague in the skin of the body: and if the hair in the plague has turned white, and the appearance of the plague is deeper than the body’s skin, it is the plague of leprosy; and the priest shall examine him, and pronounce him unclean.
If the bright spot is white in the skin of his body, and its appearance isn’t deeper than the skin, and its hair hasn’t turned white, then the priest shall isolate the infected person for seven days.
The priest shall examine him on the seventh day, and, behold, if in his eyes the plague is arrested, and the plague hasn’t spread in the skin, then the priest shall isolate him for seven more days.

The priest shall examine him again on the seventh day; and behold, if the plague has faded, and the plague hasn’t spread in the skin, then the priest shall pronounce him clean. It is a scab. He shall wash his clothes, and be clean.
But if the scab spreads on the skin, after he has shown himself to the priest for his cleansing, he shall show himself to the priest again.
The priest shall examine him; and behold, if the scab has spread on the skin, then the priest shall pronounce him unclean. It is leprosy.
“When the plague of leprosy is in a man, then he shall be brought to the priest;
and the priest shall examine him. Behold, if there is a white rising in the skin, and it has turned the hair white, and there is raw flesh in the rising,
it is a chronic leprosy in the skin of his body, and the priest shall pronounce him unclean. He shall not isolate him, for he is already unclean.
“If the leprosy breaks out all over the skin, and the leprosy covers all the skin of the infected person from his head even to his feet, as far as it appears to the priest;
then the priest shall examine him; and, behold, if the leprosy has covered all his flesh, he shall pronounce him clean of the plague. It has all turned white: he is clean.
But whenever raw flesh appears in him, he shall be unclean.
The priest shall examine the raw flesh, and pronounce him unclean: the raw flesh is unclean. It is leprosy.
Or if the raw flesh turns again, and is changed to white, then he shall come to the priest;
and the priest shall examine him; and, behold, if the plague has turned white, then the priest shall pronounce him clean of the plague. He is clean.
“When the body has a boil on its skin, and it has healed,
and in the place of the boil there is a white rising, or a bright spot, reddish-white, then it shall be shown to the priest;

and the priest shall examine it; and behold, if its appearance is lower than the skin, and its hair has turned white, then the priest shall pronounce him unclean. It is the plague of leprosy. It has broken out in the boil.
But if the priest examines it, and behold, there are no white hairs in it, and it isn’t deeper than the skin, but is dim, then the priest shall isolate him seven days.
If it spreads in the skin, then the priest shall pronounce him unclean. It is a plague.
But if the bright spot stays in its place, and hasn’t spread, it is the scar from the boil; and the priest shall pronounce him clean.
“Or when the body has a burn from fire on its skin, and the raw flesh of the burn becomes a bright spot, reddish-white, or white,

then the priest shall examine it; and behold, if the hair in the bright spot has turned white, and its appearance is deeper than the skin; it is leprosy. It has broken out in the burning, and the priest shall pronounce him unclean. It is the plague of leprosy.
But if the priest examines it, and behold, there is no white hair in the bright spot, and it isn’t lower than the skin, but is faded; then the priest shall isolate him seven days.
The priest shall examine him on the seventh day. If it has spread in the skin, then the priest shall pronounce him unclean. It is the plague of leprosy.
If the bright spot stays in its place, and hasn’t spread in the skin, but is faded, it is the swelling from the burn, and the priest shall pronounce him clean; for it is the scar from the burn.
“When a man or woman has a plague on the head or on the beard,

then the priest shall examine the plague; and behold, if its appearance is deeper than the skin, and the hair in it is yellow and thin, then the priest shall pronounce him unclean: it is an itch, it is leprosy of the head or of the beard.

If the priest examines the plague of itching, and behold, its appearance isn’t deeper than the skin, and there is no black hair in it, then the priest shall isolate the person infected with itching seven days.
On the seventh day the priest shall examine the plague; and behold, if the itch hasn’t spread, and there is no yellow hair in it, and the appearance of the itch isn’t deeper than the skin,
then he shall be shaved, but he shall not shave the itch; and the priest shall shut him up who has the itch seven more days.

On the seventh day, the priest shall examine the itch; and behold, if the itch hasn’t spread in the skin, and its appearance isn’t deeper than the skin, then the priest shall pronounce him clean. He shall wash his clothes, and be clean.
But if the itch spreads in the skin after his cleansing,
then the priest shall examine him; and behold, if the itch has spread in the skin, the priest shall not look for the yellow hair; he is unclean.
But if in his eyes the itch is arrested, and black hair has grown in it; the itch is healed, he is clean. The priest shall pronounce him clean.
“When a man or a woman has bright spots in the skin of the body, even white bright spots;
then the priest shall examine them; and behold, if the bright spots on the skin of their body are a dull white, it is a harmless rash, it has broken out in the skin; he is clean.
“If a man’s hair has fallen from his head, he is bald. He is clean.
If his hair has fallen off from the front part of his head, he is forehead bald. He is clean.
But if there is in the bald head, or the bald forehead, a reddish-white plague; it is leprosy breaking out in his bald head, or his bald forehead.
Then the priest shall examine him; and, behold, if the rising of the plague is reddish-white in his bald head, or in his bald forehead, like the appearance of leprosy in the skin of the flesh,
he is a leprous man. He is unclean. The priest shall surely pronounce him unclean. His plague is on his head.
“The leper in whom the plague is shall wear torn clothes, and the hair of his head shall hang loose. He shall cover his upper lip, and shall cry, ‘Unclean! Unclean!’
All the days in which the plague is in him he shall be unclean. He is unclean. He shall dwell alone. Outside of the camp shall be his dwelling.
“The garment also that the plague of leprosy is in, whether it is a woolen garment, or a linen garment;
whether it is in warp, or woof; of linen, or of wool; whether in a skin, or in anything made of skin;
if the plague is greenish or reddish in the garment, or in the skin, or in the warp, or in the woof, or in anything made of skin; it is the plague of leprosy, and shall be shown to the priest.
The priest shall examine the plague, and isolate the plague seven days.

He shall examine the plague on the seventh day. If the plague has spread in the garment, either in the warp, or in the woof, or in the skin, whatever use the skin is used for, the plague is a destructive mildew. It is unclean.
He shall burn the garment, whether the warp or the woof, in wool or in linen, or anything of skin, in which the plague is: for it is a destructive mildew. It shall be burned in the fire.
“If the priest examines it, and behold, the plague hasn’t spread in the garment, either in the warp, or in the woof, or in anything of skin;
then the priest shall command that they wash the thing in which the plague is, and he shall isolate it seven more days.

Then the priest shall examine it, after the plague is washed; and behold, if the plague hasn’t changed its color, and the plague hasn’t spread, it is unclean; you shall burn it in the fire. It is a mildewed spot, whether the bareness is inside or outside.
If the priest looks, and behold, the plague has faded after it is washed, then he shall tear it out of the garment, or out of the skin, or out of the warp, or out of the woof:
and if it appears again in the garment, either in the warp, or in the woof, or in anything of skin, it is spreading. You shall burn with fire that in which the plague is.
The garment, either the warp, or the woof, or whatever thing of skin it is, which you shall wash, if the plague has departed from them, then it shall be washed the second time, and it will be clean.”
This is the law of the plague of mildew in a garment of wool or linen, either in the warp, or the woof, or in anything of skin, to pronounce it clean, or to pronounce it unclean.

footnotes.content: God gives His instructions to the leaders—Moses and Aaron together. This is how His word reaches us: through those He calls to shepherd. Even in laws about sickness and separation, the Lord speaks with care.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The person with a concerning skin mark 'shall be brought to Aaron the priest.' Suspicion alone doesn't declare the matter—it must be examined carefully by someone appointed to see. We too need counsel when we're uncertain.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The priest looks at four things: the skin mark, the hair's color, how deep it sits, and the person's eyes. Such particular attention! God's law doesn't rush judgment. Careful examination honors the person being examined.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Seven days of isolation—not as punishment, but as pause. The priest doesn't declare 'unclean' at first glance. There's room for waiting, for watching, for the body to speak its own truth over time.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: 'The plague is arrested'—it hasn't spread. One week passes, and hope remains. The priest examines again on the seventh day, watching for stillness rather than motion. Sometimes what matters most is what does NOT happen.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The plague fades, and the person is pronounced clean. Wash your clothes, return to community. This is mercy written into the law—the possibility of healing and restoration, not endless exile.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: But if the mark spreads after cleansing, the person must show himself again. Hidden deterioration isn't left hidden. Truth eventually surfaces, and we must face it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The spread is seen; the pronouncement is clear. 'It is leprosy.' Sometimes after all the waiting, the answer comes—not the one we hoped for, but definite. In such clarity, we at least know where we stand.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Another case: the unmistakable leprosy. The person is brought to the priest. No ambiguity here. Some conditions announce themselves plainly, and meeting them honestly is an act of faith.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Three signs together: the white rising, hair turned white, raw flesh. The body speaks. The priest reads what he sees. Before we can be healed, we must acknowledge what is.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: 'He shall not isolate him, for he is already unclean.' The progression is complete—no quarantine needed now, only acknowledgment. Sometimes the kindest word we can speak is the truth.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: When leprosy breaks out everywhere—the entire skin whitened. A complete reversal of the world's logic, yet here it opens a door toward healing. Sometimes fullness, not emptiness, is what begins restoration.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: 'It has all turned white: he is clean.' This puzzling pronouncement teaches us—God's law looks deeper than surface assessment. What appears wholly destroyed may be healed.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: But raw flesh appearing breaks the picture—a return of the sore, unhealed place. The presence of rawness within what seemed whole resets everything. Hidden hurt often speaks loudest.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The priest sees the raw flesh and speaks: 'unclean. It is leprosy.' The rawness is the marker. We cannot pretend wholeness over wounded places.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: But if the raw flesh heals—turns white again—there is one more chance. The door opens once more for restoration. Hope lingers even after many turns.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The priest examines and the pronouncement comes: clean. Healing is real. The law grants what the body's restoration merits—freedom and return.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A boil on the skin, and it heals. Wounds do mend. New skin grows. Yet even in healing, a question remains: what mark does it leave?
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: In the place of healing, a rising or bright spot appears. Sometimes what grows after a wound is not what we expected. The place that was broken requires watching still.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The priest sees white hairs and depth; the plague 'has broken out in the boil.' What we thought was healing was disguise. The old wound spoke, unhealed beneath.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: But no white hairs, shallow, and dim—this mark is not the plague. Seven days again to be certain. The Lord's law gives second glances to those who need them.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: If it spreads, the plague is declared. Motion tells the story. A spreading mark cannot hide its nature.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: But the bright spot stays still—it stays in its place. Then it is the scar from the boil, and the person is clean. Stillness itself becomes proof of healing.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A burn from fire, and raw flesh becomes a bright spot. Even in the place of injury, new marks appear. The body's story is written in marks, and each tells something true.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: White hairs in the spot, depth beneath the skin—the priest sees and pronounces: leprosy broke out in the burning. Even what came from fire can carry deeper sickness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: No white hairs, not deeper, but faded—the mark will be watched. Seven days of waiting again. The kindness of repetition, the offer of another chance.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: On the seventh day, if it has spread, the plague is declared. Time reveals what was hidden. We live in time; truth lives there too.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The bright spot stays still, faded—it is the swelling from the burn, and the person is clean. The mark of injury is not shame; healing is real.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A plague on the head or beard—the place where identity shows. Here too, careful watching. No part of us is overlooked by the law's mercy.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Yellow, thin hair and depth speak of the itch—a leprosy specific to head or beard. Even in what touches our identity and appearance, the law names what is and offers a path forward.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Not deeper, no black hair—wait. Seven days of isolation. Even on the head, patience is offered before a final word.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: On the seventh day, examine again. The itch hasn't spread, no yellow hair, not deeper. The signs are read carefully, point by point.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Shave the surrounding hair, but not the itch itself. Let it be seen clearly. Honesty about our condition comes before healing.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Seven more days. Then if the itch hasn't spread and isn't deeper, the person is clean. Wash your clothes. Return. Welcome home.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: But if the itch spreads after cleansing, the journey begins again. Disappointment lives in these verses too—the moment hope falls away.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The priest examines; the itch has spread. He doesn't search for yellow hair now—the verdict is already clear. When truth is plain, we stop looking for loopholes.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: But if the itch is arrested and black hair grows—the itch is healed. The person is clean. Nature itself offers healing; the law receives and declares it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Bright spots on the skin—white, appearing on man or woman alike. The law doesn't distinguish here; both are examined with the same care.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Dull white spots—a harmless rash, not the plague. Sometimes what alarms us is nothing to fear. The priest's examination brings relief.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: 'If a man's hair has fallen from his head, he is bald. He is clean.' Simple, absolute—losing hair is not a sign of uncleanness. Some natural losses are simply loss, nothing more.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Hair fallen from the front—forehead bald. Clean. The law grants dignity to aging, to change. What the body does naturally is not sin.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: But a reddish-white plague on the bald head—leprosy breaking out. Here is where the distinction matters. Even in baldness, the plague announces itself.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The priest examines the reddish-white rising, comparing it to leprosy in the flesh elsewhere. Careful comparison: what does this look like, and what does that look like? Truth stands between them.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A leprous man, unclean. The plague is on his head. The pronouncement comes. There is weight in these words, and also finality—we are not left wondering.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: 'Unclean! Unclean!' The leper cries out his own condition—torn clothes, loose hair, covered lip. He becomes the herald of his own separation. Even in exile, his voice remains.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: All the days the plague is in him, he dwells alone, outside the camp. The law is clear about exile but also—crucially—provisional. 'All the days'—implying the day might come when he returns.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Now the law turns to garments—cloth that the plague can touch. Even our belongings matter; the Lord's holiness extends to the things we wear.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Warp, woof, linen, wool, skin—every kind of material is named. Nothing escapes the law's jurisdiction. Completeness is given here.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Greenish or reddish in the garment—the plague announces itself in color. What we wear speaks. What clings to us is worthy of examination.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The priest examines the garment and isolates it—seven days of watching, even for cloth. Patience is shown to things as well as to people.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: If it spreads—warp, woof, skin—'it is a destructive mildew. It is unclean.' The plague's nature is that it spreads. Motion marks its character.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Burn it in the fire. What cannot be cleansed is consumed. Sometimes mercy means ending, not mending. Fire returns things to dust.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: But if the plague hasn't spread—if it is still, contained. Then another path opens. The distinction between what spreads and what stays is everything.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Wash the garment and isolate it seven more days. Cleansing work is offered. The thing might be made whole again.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: After washing, examine again. If the color hasn't changed and the plague hasn't spread—the thing is unclean still. Washing alone was not enough. Some conditions persist.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: But if the plague has faded after washing, tear it out—remove the contaminated part. Partial recovery means partial salvation; what can be saved is preserved.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: If it appears again, spreading—burn it. A second chance, refused by the plague itself. Sometimes returning corruption must be met with finality.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Wash it a second time—if the plague departed, it will be clean. The law permits a second washing, a second hope. Restoration is offered more than once.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Readers today hear an echo in this closing instruction: clear law given for the hardest cases—how to tell the truly sick from the worried well, the permanent stain from the washable mark. As of 2026-10, we still need such discernment.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
